topic_and_scope: Assessment of health, healthcare costs, and productivity impacts of halting the rise of overweight and obesity in Kenya by 2025 using the Kenya Obesity Model (proportional multistate life table), comparing a 2025 stabilization scenario with a delayed 2044 stabilization scenario.
main_themes: Health and economic impact of obesity prevention in a low- and middle-income country (LMIC) context
Methodological approach and data requirements of a national obesity model (pMSLT) and its policy relevance
Policy implications and data gaps for obesity prevention in Kenya and similar settings
main_findings: Halting the rise of overweight and obesity by 2025 could yield about 6.8 million health-adjusted life years (HALYs) over the lifetime of the 2019 Kenyan population (135 HALYs per 1000 persons), with substantial gains emerging over time.

By 2044, the intervention could save about US$755 million in healthcare costs and realize about US$5.8 billion in productivity gains (combined mortality and morbidity effects), underscoring that productivity gains may vastly exceed direct healthcare cost savings.

key_gaps.description: Costs for multiple BMI-related diseases in Kenya are missing or limited to hospital-based estimates (e.g., low back pain, osteoarthritis, gout, Alzheimer’s and other dementias, cataract, gallbladder and biliary diseases, and atrial fibrillation), likely leading to underestimation of total cost savings.

The model uses a closed cohort with no birth cohort addition or county-level socioeconomic stratification, and applies a single wage rate across ages and sexes, reducing precision for equity and long-term projections.

future_directions.title: Add county- and socioeconomic-stratified modelling to the Kenya Obesity Model
future_directions.rationale: National-level estimates mask substantial heterogeneity in obesity prevalence, disease burden, costs, and productivity across Kenya's counties and socioeconomic groups. Incorporating county-level data for BMI, disease incidence, per-capita healthcare costs, and employment can reveal where interventions have the greatest impact and how to allocate resources more efficiently. Steps include compiling county-specific BMI and disease data, adapting the model to run parallel sub-models, and presenting results as county-focused scenarios to guide targeted policies and investments.

future_directions.title: Incorporate birth cohorts and population dynamics into the model
future_directions.rationale: The current analysis uses a closed 2019 cohort; incorporating birth rates, fertility trends, and migration will alter future BMI exposure, disease incidence, and lifetime costs. A dynamic population module should integrate age-structured birth cohorts and potential immigration to capture long-term effects of obesity prevention on new generations. This will enhance the realism of lifetime HALYs, costs, and productivity projections and improve policy planning for multiple decades.

future_directions.title: Update and expand disease-cost data for additional BMI-associated conditions in Kenya
future_directions.rationale: Several BMI-associated conditions lack Kenya-specific cost data, and existing estimates are hospital-based and may overrepresent advanced disease costs. New primary costing studies should cover musculoskeletal conditions (e.g., low back pain, OA), cataract, gout, and atrial fibrillation, including outpatient and private-sector costs. Incorporating comorbidity and variation by disease stage will improve accuracy of cost savings, inform cost-effectiveness analyses, and strengthen policy justification.

future_directions.title: Assess cost-effectiveness of specific policy interventions within the model
future_directions.rationale: Policy options such as sugar-sweetened beverage taxes, kilojoule menu labeling, and reformulation targets have shown potential in other settings. Running scenario analyses that implement these policies to modify BMI trajectories will yield incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) and budget impact estimates. The goal is to identify dominant or highly cost-saving strategies and provide clear guidance for prioritizing interventions that maximize health, cost savings, and productivity gains.

future_directions.title: Assess equity effects across sex, age, urban/rural residence, and wealth quintiles
future_directions.rationale: Obesity and its health/economic consequences may disproportionately affect certain groups. Disaggregating results will reveal whether interventions reduce or exacerbate health and economic inequalities. The next step is to collect and integrate disaggregated data by sex, age bands, residence, and socioeconomic status, and to run equity-focused scenario analyses to inform inclusive policy design.

future_directions.title: Incorporate broader productivity channels, including older age groups and the informal sector
future_directions.rationale: Kenyan productivity is not limited to formal employment; older workers and informal sector participants contribute economically. Extending the productive-age range beyond 65 and incorporating informal sector earnings will yield a more comprehensive estimate of total productivity gains. This requires data on formal/informal employment composition and age-specific productivity metrics to refine WA inputs.

future_directions.title: Model multiple wage-growth and macroeconomic scenarios to test robustness of productivity gains
future_directions.rationale: Productivity estimates are sensitive to wage trajectories and macroeconomic conditions. Incorporating scenarios with varying wage growth, unemployment, and inflation will test the stability of productivity gains under different economic futures. The analyses should report a range of outcomes and identify conditions under which the economic case for obesity prevention remains strongest.

future_directions.title: Develop a user-friendly decision-support tool for policymakers and stakeholders
future_directions.rationale: To translate complex model outputs into actionable policy, create an interactive dashboard that allows county-level inputs, disease-specific outcomes, and policy scenario adjustments. Such a tool would support iterative policy planning, enable rapid re-analysis as new data become available, and facilitate stakeholder engagement and transparent decision-making.
